items.title: What hoisting PollyClient to module scope buys
items.body:
The key is right: reuse of the client, its credential resolver and its connections across requests. In v1, `new PollyClient(...)` is inside the `/speak` handler, so every request builds a fresh client, a fresh credential resolver and a fresh HTTP agent. Moving that one line to module scope (top of the file, run once) means every request shares one client, and the SDK can keep connections open and reuse them. The guide calls it a one-line change; it is STORY-03.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Lets Polly accept more than 3000 characters": 3000 billed characters is Polly's hard limit per call; where you create the client cannot change it.
- "Required for `AudioStream.pipe(res)`": streaming works either way; the issue is only cost per request.
- "Makes voice and engine configurable per request": those are parameters of each call, not of the client.

excerpts.quote: The `new PollyClient(...)` inside the handler builds a fresh client, credential resolver and HTTP agent on **every request**. Hoisting it to module scope is a one-line change and lets the SDK reuse connections
Polly's hard limit is 3000 billed characters per `SynthesizeSpeech` call

items.title: Why the presigner's service name must be "transcribe"
items.body:
The key is right: you get an opaque 403 on WebSocket connect, because the signing name must be `transcribe`. A SigV4 signature includes the **service name**, and AWS checks it. For Transcribe streaming, the hostname starts with `transcribestreaming`, but the signing name is just `transcribe`. If you sign with the hostname's name, the signature AWS computes does not match yours, and the WebSocket is refused with a 403 that does not say why ("opaque").

Why the others are wrong:
- "The URL expires immediately": expiry is set separately by `expiresIn: 300`, five minutes.
- "A DNS failure": the hostname is not rebuilt from the signing name; the connection reaches AWS and is then refused.
- "Nothing changes": the guide lists this as a mistake with a concrete symptom.

excerpts.quote: **`service: "transcribe"`** — not `"transcribestreaming"`. The signing service name and the hostname prefix differ. Getting this wrong produces an opaque 403 on WebSocket connect.
**`expiresIn: 300`** — the URL is dead after five minutes.

items.title: The assumption behind content[0].text
items.body:
The key is right: the line assumes the first content block is a text block. In the Messages API, `responseBody.content` is not a string; it is an **array of content blocks**, and each block has a type. For a plain text reply, block 0 is a text block, so `content[0].text` works. If a reply ever started with a block that is not text, `.text` would not be there. The guide calls it a load-bearing assumption: the code silently depends on it.

Why the others are wrong:
- "That content is a string": the code indexes `content[0]`, which treats it as an array.
- "That anthropic_version names the model": the guide says `anthropic_version` is the wire-format version, not the model version, and this line does not read it.
- "Exactly one output token": token count has nothing to do with the shape of `content`.

excerpts.quote: Note the shape of the response: `responseBody.content` is an **array of content blocks**, and the code assumes `content[0]` is a text block. That is true for a plain text reply, but it is a load-bearing assumption.
`anthropic_version: 'bedrock-2023-05-31'` is the wire-format version Bedrock requires in the body — it is not the model version.

items.title: Why an async onaudioprocess handler can reorder audio
items.body:
The key is right: the browser does not wait for the callback, so two in flight can send audio out of order. `onaudioprocess` fires on a fixed rhythm. Marking it `async` and awaiting `resampleTo16kHz` means the function returns a promise immediately, and the browser fires the next callback on time whether or not the last one finished. If a later chunk resamples faster, its `socket.send()` can happen first, and the transcript is corrupted. Because the `AudioContext` is already 16 kHz, the branch rarely runs, and the guide warns that "rarely" is the worst kind of bug.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Flips the endianness": byte order is set by `floatTo16BitPCM`, not by timing.
- "Blocks the WebSocket from receiving": `await` pauses only that function; nothing is blocked.
- "Runs only once": the browser keeps calling it; that is exactly why calls can overlap.

excerpts.quote: processor.onaudioprocess = async e => { if (audioContext.sampleRate !== 16000) { input = await resampleTo16kHz(input, audioContext.sampleRate);

`onaudioprocess` fires on a fixed cadence and does not wait for the previous promise. If two callbacks are ever in flight, their `socket.send()` calls can land out of order, which corrupts the transcript.

items.title: Which part of an event-stream frame is little-endian
items.body:
The key is right: only the PCM samples in the payload are little-endian; the framing is big-endian. **Endianness** is the byte order of a multi-byte number: big-endian puts the most significant byte first, little-endian the least significant first. In an AWS event-stream frame, the prelude (total length, headers length), the prelude CRC, the header length fields and the message CRC are all big-endian. The audio inside the payload is raw 16-bit PCM, which Transcribe wants little-endian. The guide calls mixing these up the classic bug in this code path.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Only the two CRC32 checksums": the checksums are part of the big-endian framing.
- "Everything, because Web Audio is little-endian": the frame layout is explicitly marked BE.
- "Only the prelude length fields": the diagram marks exactly those fields as BE.

excerpts.quote: Everything here is **big-endian** except the PCM samples inside the payload, which are **little-endian**. Mixing those up is the classic bug in this code path.
│ 4 bytes (BE)   │ 4 bytes (BE)     │ 4 bytes      │ N bytes │ M bytes │ 4 bytes      │
Transcribe wants 16-bit signed little-endian PCM at 16 kHz, mono.

items.title: Why v1 brokers Transcribe access, and what it costs
items.body:
The key is right: proxying would mean relaying every audio chunk, and the cost is five minutes of unmetered AWS access. Transcribe streaming is a long-lived, two-way connection. To proxy it, the server would have to pass along every 4096-sample chunk in both directions. Handing out a signed URL is simpler and faster. But anyone who can reach `/get-signed-url` gets a URL that works for five minutes, straight against your AWS account, with nothing counting or limiting their use. Fine on localhost; a real problem in production, which STORY-04 addresses with CORS and rate limits.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Transcribe rejects server IPs": the guide gives no such reason.
- "Browsers cannot open WebSockets to localhost": the issue is relaying audio, not localhost.
- "Signed URLs are cheaper; you lose partial results": partial results still arrive over the direct WebSocket.

excerpts.quote: The broker pattern exists because Transcribe streaming is a long-lived bidirectional connection — proxying it would mean the server relaying every 4096-sample audio chunk.
The tradeoff is that anyone who can reach `/get-signed-url` gets five minutes of direct, unmetered access to your AWS Transcribe account.

items.title: Why the x-amzn-transcribe headers are left out of the signature
items.body:
The key is right: a browser WebSocket cannot send custom headers, so a signature over them would never match. A SigV4 signature covers the parts of the request it lists. The browser's `WebSocket` API only lets you give a URL; you cannot add your own headers. So if the `x-amzn-transcribe-*` headers were part of the signature, AWS would compute the signature over a request that never carried them, and it would fail. The code lists them as `unsignableHeaders`, and the same settings travel as **query-string parameters**, which the browser can send.

Why the others are wrong:
- "They carry the secret key": they carry settings like language and sample rate, not credentials.
- "AWS forbids signing x-amzn headers": the guide gives the browser limit as the reason, not an AWS rule.
- "Keeps the URL short": length is not mentioned; the issue is matching.

excerpts.quote: but a browser `WebSocket` cannot send custom headers. If they were signed, the signature would never match what the browser actually sends, so they are explicitly excluded from the signature and the equivalent query-string parameters do the real work.

items.title: The three v1 endpoints and what each one talks to
items.body:
v1 is one Express server with three HTML pages and three API endpoints, one per AWS service. Learn this map first; every quiz hangs off one of these paths.

- **Text-to-Speech**: the page posts text to `POST /speak`, and MP3 audio comes back.
- **Live Transcription**: the page calls `GET /get-signed-url` and then streams audio for captions.
- **Ask Claude**: the page posts a prompt to `POST /ask-claude`, and Claude's text comes back.

As you read §3 of the architecture guide, ask for each path: who holds the AWS credentials, and who actually opens the connection to AWS? The guide calls the answer "the important structural insight", and two later sections (CORS and cost) depend on it.

Also note what v1 does **not** have: no database, no build step, no framework, no tests and no authentication. Many of the §6 defects follow from that last point.

excerpts.quote: A single Express server (`server.js`, ~220 lines) serves three static HTML pages from `public/` and exposes three API endpoints.
- **Text-to-Speech** → `POST /speak` → AWS Polly → MP3 audio streamed back
There is no database, no build step, no framework, no tests, and no auth.

items.title: Why the v1 pages 404 when started from another folder
items.body:
The key is right: they 404, because the path resolves against the current working directory, not `server.js`. `express.static('public')` uses a relative path. Node resolves relative paths against the folder the process was **started from** (the working directory), not the folder the script lives in. Start the server from the parent directory and Express looks for `./public` there, finds nothing, and silently returns 404 for every page. The guide's fix: `express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'public'))`, where `__dirname` is always the script's own folder.

Why the others are wrong:
- "Falls back to node_modules": Express has no such fallback.
- "Refuses to start": a missing static folder is not an error at startup; the guide says the files *silently* 404.
- "Load normally, relative to the entry file": that is what the guide says does **not** happen.

excerpts.quote: `express.static('public')` resolves relative to the **process working directory**, not to `server.js`. Start the server from anywhere other than the repo root and the static files silently 404.
Prefer `express.static(path.join(__dirname, 'public'))`.

items.title: Start here: Nova, a voice assistant with a retired v1 kept beside v2
items.body:
Nova is a small voice assistant built on three AWS services: **Polly** (text to speech), **Transcribe** (live speech to text) and **Claude on Bedrock** (the conversation). The repo has an unusual shape: the original version (v1, `server.js` and `public/*.html` at the root) is commented out but kept, and the rewrite (v2) lives in `app/`.

All the quizzes in this pack are about **v1**, as described in the architecture guide. Suggested reading order:

1. The root `README.md` (the "Start here" table and the note about the retired v1).
2. `fabledocs/README.md`: its status note, the TL;DR of the app and the glossary.
3. `fabledocs/01-architecture.md`, in order: the summary and diagram (§1-3), the `server.js` walkthrough (§4), the front end and its three concepts (§5), then the known issues (§6).

Read §4 and §5 slowly: the "things a junior engineer will trip over" lists and the concept boxes are where most quiz material comes from. Then try exercise 1 in `fabledocs/README.md`: pick a defect from §6 and find how `app/` fixes it.

excerpts.quote: `server.js` and `public/*.html` at the repository root are the original implementation. They are commented out in full rather than deleted
This repo's unusual asset: **v1 is still here, commented out, next to the v2 that replaced it.**

The full v1 walkthrough and its nine known issues.

items.title: Why every Ask Claude request in v1 shows "Error."
items.body:
The key is right: `server.js` calls `JSON.parse` on the raw prompt string, which throws, and the handler returns 500. `claude.html` sends `{ prompt: input }`, where `input` is plain text like `what is 2+2`. The server then runs `JSON.parse(req.body.prompt ?? '')`, expecting a JSON array of messages. Plain text is not valid JSON, so it throws inside the `try`, the `catch` returns `500 {"error": "Error calling Claude"}`, and the page renders "Error.". The guide traces this to commit `f8dba37`, which changed the server without updating the page: a broken **contract** between front end and back end.

Why the others are wrong:
- "The model ID expired, 404": the request never reaches Bedrock; it fails on the parse line.
- "Bedrock rejects short prompts": again, Bedrock is never called.
- "CORS blocks it": v1 uses `cors()` for any origin, and the page is served by the same server.

excerpts.quote: body: JSON.stringify({ prompt: input })     // input === "what is 2+2"
messages: JSON.parse(req.body.prompt ?? '')
So every request from the browser throws inside the `try` block, gets caught, and returns `500 {"error": "Error calling Claude"}` — the page renders "Error.".

items.title: How to treat a partial Transcribe result
items.body:
The key is right: treat it as a running guess that gets replaced, not appended to the final transcript. Transcribe sends its best guess continuously while you speak. `IsPartial: true` means "this will change": the next message may correct words. `IsPartial: false` means "this is settled", and only then is the text appended to the output. v1 writes partial results into the status line and appends final ones to the `pre` element, which the guide calls the right split.

Why the others are wrong:
- "As final text; Transcribe only sends confident results": the guide says the opposite; partial results change.
- "An error frame; close the socket": partial results are the normal stream, not errors.
- "A duplicate of the previous final result": a partial result is newer than the last final one; it is the start of the next phrase.

excerpts.quote: Transcribe emits its running best guess continuously. `IsPartial: true` means "this will change" — the current code writes it into the status line. `IsPartial: false` means "this is settled" — the code appends it to the output
It gets replaced as more audio arrives. A result with `IsPartial: false` is final.

items.title: How to read the v1 walkthrough and its defect list
items.body:
The architecture guide is written for a junior engineer, and it repeats one pattern: show a few lines of v1, then explain what is subtle about them. To get the most from it:

- **Keep the glossary open.** Terms like SigV4, presigned URL, PCM and event stream appear without re-explanation. Look each one up the first time you meet it, and note what it means for who can call AWS and for how long.
- **Read the "trip over" bullets as rules.** Each one names a value (a service name, a header list, an expiry time) and says what breaks if you get it wrong.
- **For each defect in §6, find three things**: the exact line in v1, the severity the guide gives it, and the story that fixes it. Some are about correctness (a request that always fails), some about security or cost, and some about rare timing problems.

A good self-test: for every v1 line the guide quotes, say what *assumption* it makes. Several quizzes ask exactly that.

excerpts.quote: Things a junior engineer will trip over here:
Ordered roughly by severity. Each maps to a story in [02-user-stories.md](./02-user-stories.md).

items.title: How /get-signed-url differs from /speak and /ask-claude
items.body:
The key is right: `/get-signed-url` is a **credential broker**. The server signs a URL and hands it to the browser; the browser then talks to AWS directly over a WebSocket, and the server is out of the loop. `/speak` and `/ask-claude` are the opposite pattern, a **proxy**: the browser never touches AWS, and the server holds the credentials, makes the call and relays the result.

Why the others are wrong:
- "It is a proxy too, relaying every chunk": the guide says the broker pattern exists precisely to avoid relaying every audio chunk.
- "The only endpoint that requires sign-in": v1 has no auth at all.
- "Hands the AWS secret key to the browser": the browser gets a signed URL, not the key. The signature lets the holder make that call without holding the credentials.

excerpts.quote: `/get-signed-url` is a **credential broker**. The server signs a URL and hands it over; the browser then talks to AWS *directly* over a WebSocket, with the server completely out of the loop.
`/speak` and `/ask-claude` are a **proxy**. The browser never touches AWS.
so the holder can call AWS without holding the credentials.
